doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Aging brass players, expedience and Maynard Ferguson
summary: On losing physical skill, Jimmy cites his service training in expedience and talks of Maynard Ferguson's chops, first seen when Jimmy was thirteen at Crystal Beach.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Do you think it sometimes comes from knowing how to deal with perhaps the diminishing physical skill at what they do? Like let’s say a trumpet player has made his mark as a high note man, right? And it gets to the point where they can’t quite get up to
where they used to. And unless they can figure out, well I can’t quite do that but I can do—
That’s where the decision comes in.
That’s where the decision comes see. And most guys don’t make it.

Yeah. Because in a sense, in terms of dealing with the attitude of achieving, it’s like they don’t seem to have arrived at the attitude of dealing with the art of feeling expedience. Do you know what I mean when I say that? I learned that from the service. In other words, you’re out in the wilderness. You don’t know anything about the wilderness. But at the same time, you go through all your agony etcetera, and pretty soon, bang, that creative energy coming from all that environment plus yourself, tells you what to do because you stopped to listen. And you listen and you act on it. So it’s the same thing, in a sense, when you’re playing. If you don’t listen to what you’re playing, if you don’t hear what you’re playing, then you’re a trained robot, technically, mechanically, like mass production, bing-bing-bing-bing. But there is no spirit involved in terms of equating to soul expression, feeling. It’s all intellectual.
They have to find a part for themselves once they break down like that.
Because being around a lot of lead players, and at the same time as a soloist — like you take Maynard Ferguson. Now, lead player, solo and everything, “chops a mile.”

He was born with that. I saw him when I was thirteen years old. His mother and father would escort him at the Crystal Beach you know, with his band you see? You follow me? He had it. But everybody else who finally heard him, assumed whatever they wanted to assume, of how he got that way. He was born to do what he do. Like when I got in the band, he had five trumpets.
And they were trying to beat Maynard. And they’re trying to beat every note.

Up high, that’s the point, see? Not out-jazz him. They’re trying to — see that’s where all the high stuff comes in you see. They’re trying to out-high him, and the lead player is trying to warn him, because they’re youngsters you know.
Oh, they’re arrogant and everything, they didn’t want to hear it.
“You don’t know what you’re talking about old man.”

See Maynard is still moving around, playing, no matter how somebody want to criticize, why he doesn’t have the chops he used to, well heck, the person talking don’t have what they had. That’s why the tune was written “Things Ain’t What They Used to Be.” That’s the main reason why it was written, believe me. So that’s where that whole thing kind of comes in, in terms of dealing with that attitude about the whole thing. Because if that was the goal, the top goal, just to be a high note player, well then eventually you’ll run out,

you don’t even have too much of dealing with the law of permutation. In other words, to make do with what you’ve got. That’s why I’ll get back to the theory of expedience. In other words you’ll find out — and naturally, you make do with what you’ve got. All of a sudden you get sensitized and you know which is poison and which isn’t. Because you’ve got to eat. Well how did you survive? Well I ate bugs, I ate this bug and I ate that bug, and then I ate this one and it made me sick so I know not to mess with that again because, you know, and if I recognize that it means I’m still living so that’s what I’m after. So you follow me?
